A '''slater''', or '''slate mason''',<ref>{{cite book|title=Quantities; a Text-book for Surveyors, in Tabulated Form|url=https://archive.org/details/quantitiesatext00fletgoog|author=Sir Banister Fletcher, Herbert Phillips Fletcher|pages=[https://archive.org/details/quantitiesatext00fletgoog/page/n45 23]|date=1888|publisher=B. T. Batsford|isbn= 1561582115}}</ref> is a [[tradesman|tradesperson]] who covers buildings with [[slate]].<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|encyclopedia=Cyclopædia of Useful Arts & Manufactures|editor=C. Tomlinson|date=1852|pages=636|article=SLATE}}</ref>

== Tools used ==
The various [[hand tool|tool]]s of the slater's trade are all [[drop-forged]].<ref name=RoofingHandbook>{{cite book|page=289|title=Roofing Handbook|author=Robert Scharff and Terry Kennedy|date=2000|publisher=McGraw-Hill Professional|isbn=0071360581}}</ref>

The slater's hammer is forged in one single piece, from crucible-cast steel, and has a {{convert|12|in|cm|0|adj=on}} leather handle. It consists of a claw for drawing nails, a sheer edge for cutting slate, and a head with a sharp point at one end for punching holes in slate and with a hammer head at the other.<ref name=RoofingHandbook /><ref name=Roofing>{{cite book|title=Roofing|author=Taunton Press Staff|page=48|date=1997|publisher=Taunton Press|isbn=1561582115}}</ref>

The ripper is also forged from crucible-cast steel and is {{convert|24|in|cm|-1}} long. It consists of a blade and a hook, and is used for removing broken slate.<ref name=RoofingHandbook /> The hook can be used to cut and remove slating nails.<ref name=RIA>{{cite book|last=Kennedy |first=Terry |title=Roofing Instant Answers |publisher=McGraw-Hill |location=New York |year=2002 |page=332 |isbn=0-07-138712-9}}</ref>

The slater's stake is T-shaped.  The vertical bar of the "T" is pointed to allow it to be driven into a rafter or other [[woodworking]] surface.  The horizontal bar of the "T" is used to support slates whilst working on them (cutting, punching, or smoothing) with other tools.  The long bar of the stake can also be used as a straight edge for marking.<ref name=RoofingHandbook /><ref name=Roofing />

The zax (also called a sack or [[Seax|sax]]<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|encyclopedia=The American Cyclopaedia: a popular dictionary of general knowledge|year=1881|first1=George|last1=Ripley|first2=Charles Anderson|last2=Dana|location=New York|url=https://archive.org/details/americancyclopae15ripl|volume=15|publisher=D. Appleton and Company|page=[https://archive.org/details/americancyclopae15ripl/page/88 88]|article=Slate}}</ref>) is a hand tool for cutting, trimming, and punching nail holes in slate. It consists of a heavy rectangular knife blade with a large point, of square cross section, protruding from the [[Axe|poll]] (or butt). The blade edge is used to split slate, while the point is used to pierce square holes for mounting the slate on the roof (with square copper nails) or making a series of small holes marking a line where the slate is broken over a slater's iron.
